title: Where Two Worlds Meet
name: Subcellular Embrace
scientific: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) of HT1080 human fibrosarcoma cells showing close associations between the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and mitochondria. In this example, ribosomes are present at the interface between these two organelles.
description: Inside every cell, tiny compartments work together to keep all the activities running. This image brings two of them into one view: the endoplasmic reticulum, which helps make proteins and lipids, and mitochondria, which produce much of the cell’s usable energy, ATP. Where these structures meet, they can exchange signals and materials.

title: The Endoplasmic Reticulum: A Network Within the cells
name: Living Network
scientific: Live-cell confocal imaging of KDEL-GFP labelled endoplasmic reticulum (ER) in COS-7 cells. Signal intensity is represented by colour coding.
description: The endoplasmic reticulum is an extensive network of membranes that spans throughout the cell. It is the site for protein synthesis, stores calcium, and participates in the cell’s response to stress. Although it looks like many separate branches, all of this subcellular structure is connected as one continuous membrane network inside the cell.

title: Mitochondria: The Cell’s Powerhouse
name: Cellular Fire
scientific: Confocal imaging of mitochondria in HT1080 human fibrosarcoma cells, labelled with an antibody against oxidative phosphorylation Complex V. Signal intensity is colour-coded in ImageJ.
description: Mitochondria are often called the cell’s powerhouses because they produce ATP, the molecule that supplies energy for many cellular activities. They are not static structures: mitochondria continually divide and fuse, changing their shape and connections. Damaged mitochondria can also be selectively removed through a process called mitophagy.

title: The Three-Dimensional Architecture of the ER
name: Hidden Layers
scientific: Three-dimensional stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), labelled with Sec61β, in COS-7 cells. Images were acquired at 100 nm Z-steps. The maximum-intensity projection combines 15 Z-slices; colour coding in Fiji represents relative Z-position.
description: A cell is not flat but it is a three-dimensional small world. To reveal its spatial organization, researchers collect a series of images at different depth and render them into a 3D view. Here, 15 of 2D section projection (maximal projection) reveal how the endoplasmic reticulum is arranged through the cell, layer by layer.

title: A Hummingbird formed by the Cytoskeleton
name: Actin Hummingbird
scientific: Wide-field fluorescence imaging of F-actin filaments in bovine pulmonary artery endothelial (BPAE) cells. F-actin was labelled with Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated phalloidin; the image was colour-coded in ImageJ.
description: The cell’s shape and movement depend in part on an internal framework called the cytoskeleton. One of its key components is F-actin, a network of protein filaments. Here, the delicate filaments resemble a hummingbird in flight. The label used to reveal them, phalloidin, binds specifically to F-actin and is derived from a poisonous mushroom.

title: A swimming cell
name: A swimming cell
scientific: Wide-field fluorescence imaging of F-actin filaments in bovine pulmonary artery endothelial (BPAE) cells. F-actin was labelled with Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated phalloidin; the image was colour-coded in ImageJ.
description: F-actin forms part of the cell’s internal support system, helping cells keep their shape, move, and organize their contents. A fluorescent dye with specific binding to F-actin makes these fine filaments visible with exposed to LED or laser. In this image, their pattern inside one cells presents a fish swimming.

title: Into the Fog of the Cytoskeleton
name: Actin Fog
scientific: Stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy of F-actin in cells. The image was deconvolved using Huygens Professional and colour-coded in Fiji.
description: Super-resolution microscopy lets researchers look beyond the limits of conventional light microscopy. STED can reveal fine structures at scales of tens of nanometres, bringing details of the cell’s internal framework into view. The delicate, glowing filaments in this image create the impression of a mysterious landscape emerging through fog.

title: A Three-Dimensional View of two subcellular structures Inside the Cell
name: Cellular Depth
scientific: Three-dimensional super-resolution (STED) imaging of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and mitochondria in HT1080 cells. The ER was labelled with ER-moxGFP (green), and mitochondria with TOMM20 (red).
description: Cells are three-dimensional, and their internal structures are arranged throughout this tiny volume. In this image, the endoplasmic reticulum appears green and mitochondria red, allowing us to see how the two structures are distributed in space. Three-dimensional imaging helps researchers move beyond a flat snapshot and explore the cell’s internal architecture.

title: The Many Shapes of the same Cell type
name: Actin Shapes
scientific: Wide-field fluorescence imaging of F-actin in BPAE cells. Signal brightness is represented by colour coding in ImageJ.
description: Cells are not all the same shape. Their outlines and internal structures reflect such diversity. This image highlights the variety of F-actin patterns across a field of cells, revealing a landscape of distinct cellular shapes.

title: A islands of Calu-3 Cells
name: Cell Clusters
scientific: Confocal imaging of Calu-3 cells labelled with DAPI for DNA in nuclei in yellow and phalloidin for F-actin in cyan.
description: Calu-3 cells are a human lung adenocarcinoma-derived cell line often used in laboratory research. Seen together, the cells form a cluster - a small community in a dish. Fluorescent labels help researchers distinguish cellular features and examine how the cells are organized.

title: A Sky Full of Cellular Stars
name: Cellular Stars
scientific: Spinning-disk confocal imaging of CellROX Green signal in HT1080 cells treated with hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂). The image was colour-coded in ImageJ to represent the detected reactive oxygen species (ROS)-associated signal.
description: Cells can experience oxidative stress when reactive oxygen species build up. In this experiment, hydrogen peroxide was used to stimulate oxidative stress, and CellROX Green helped reveal the resulting signal. The glowing pattern makes the cells look like stars scattered across a night sky.

title: When the ER Network Is Disturbed
name: Disrupted Network
scientific: Super-resolution imaging of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), labelled with ER-moxGFP, in COS-7 cells treated with nocodazole.
description: Nocodazole disrupts microtubules, part of the cell’s internal framework. Microtubules help organize the cell and support the movement of structures within it. When they are disrupted, the organization of other cellular structures, including the endoplasmic reticulum, can change. This image explores how interconnected the cell’s internal architecture can be.

title: The Ever-Changing Endoplasmic Reticulum
name: ER in Motion
scientific: Live-cell super-resolution imaging of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), labelled with ER-moxGFP, in COS-7 cells.
description: The endoplasmic reticulum is constantly moving and reshaping itself. Its tubules extend, retract, and reorganize as the cell carries out its activities. This live-cell view captures the ER as a dynamic network rather than a fixed structure.

title: When Mitochondria Join Together
name: Mitochondrial Fusion
scientific: Super-resolution imaging of mitochondria labelled with TOMM20 in COS-7 cells overexpressing mitofusin 1 (MFN1).
description: Mitochondria continually change their shape by dividing and joining together. A protein called mitofusin 1 helps mitochondria fuse. In this experiment, cells were made to produce extra MFN1, allowing researchers to examine how this protein influences the organization of the mitochondrial network.

title: The Tiny Gates to the Nucleus
name: Nuclear Gateways
scientific: Super-resolution imaging of the nuclear pore complex (NPC), labelled with Abberior STAR RED.
description: The nucleus stores the cell’s genetic instructions. Tiny structures called nuclear pore complexes sit in its surrounding membrane and act like carefully controlled gates. They regulate which molecules can enter and leave the nucleus, allowing the cell’s command centre to communicate with the rest of the cell.

title: Inside a Cell Infected by SARS-CoV-2
name: Viral Intruders
scientific: Confocal imaging of Calu-3 cells infected with SARS-CoV-2 B.1.617.2 (Delta variant). Infection induced a spheroid-like cellular phenotype. Host-cell markers show nuclei (blue) and actin (cyan); viral markers show double-stranded RNA (red) and nucleocapsid protein (yellow).
description: Viruses are too small to see with ordinary light microscopy, but researchers can use fluorescent markers to reveal viral components inside infected cells. This image shows host-cell structures alongside markers associated with SARS-CoV-2, helping researchers investigate how infection affects the appearance and organization of cells.

title: Two Proteins, One Mitochondrial Story
name: Protein Partners
scientific: Super-resolution imaging of the mitochondrial proteins MFN1 and TOMM20 in COS-7 cells overexpressing MFN1.
description: Cellular structures are built from many proteins, each with a different job. This image shows two mitochondrial proteins: MFN1, which helps mitochondria fuse, and TOMM20, a marker associated with the mitochondrial outer membrane. Viewing both together helps researchers examine the distribution of proteins within the same organelle.

title: Seeing Beyond the Diffraction Limit
name: Beyond Confocal
scientific: Comparison of confocal microscopy (red) and STED super-resolution microscopy (green) in the same region of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) in COS-7 cells. STED reveals finer details (matrices) of the ER than confocal imaging.
description: Different microscopes reveal different levels of detail. Conventional confocal microscopy is excellent for imaging cells, but very small structures can blur together. STED is a super-resolution technique that can separate finer features, allowing researchers to explore details of the endoplasmic reticulum that are difficult to distinguish with confocal microscopy.

title: The ER in Motion: 25 Frames per Second
name: Time-Lapse
scientific: Live-cell super-resolution imaging of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), labelled with ER-moxGFP, in COS-7 cells. Images were acquired at 25 frames per second.
description: The endoplasmic reticulum is always on the move. By recording 25 images every second, researchers can follow its rapid changes and watch the network rearrange in near real time. This closer view reveals just how dynamic the inside of a living cell can be.

title: A Shower of Sparks
name: Flying Sparks
description: A burst of glowing sparks rises from the campfire and disappears into the darkness. For a brief moment, each spark traces a bright, delicate path through the night-an outdoor scene that echoes the branching patterns seen in microscopy.

title: A Tapestry of Autumn Leaves
name: Autumn Layers
description: An autumn carpet of leaves becomes a natural mosaic of colour. Reds, purples, yellows, and greens overlap in layers, creating patterns and textures that are as intricate as many scenes revealed under a microscope.

title: One Network, much space
name: ER in 3D
scientific: Three-dimensional STED imaging of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), labelled with Sec61β, in COS-7 cells. Images were acquired at 100 nm Z-steps. This is a 3D rendering of a total of 71 2D sections, with colour coding in Fiji representing relative Z-position.
description: At first glance, the ER may look like a collection of countless separate branches. A 3D view helps reveal how these branches connect to form an extensive network within the cell. By combining images collected at different depths, researchers can explore this structure from a new perspective.

title: A Busy World Inside One Cell
name: Cellular Busywork
scientific: Wide-field fluorescence imaging of mitochondria (magenta), F-actin (green), and nuclei (cyan) in BPAE cells.
description: A cell is a busy place. Its nucleus contains genetic information, mitochondria help supply energy, and F-actin provides structural support. By labelling these three components in different colours, this image reveals how several essential parts are arranged within the same cell.

title: The mitochondria in the cell
name: Walking Shrimp
scientific: Supre resoultion (STED) fluorescence imaging of mitochondria in HT1080 human fibrosarcoma cells, labelled with an antibody against oxidative phosphorylation Complex V. Signal intensity is colour-coded in ImageJ.
description: Mitochondria are often called the cell’s powerhouses because they produce ATP, the molecule that supplies energy for many cellular activities. They are not static structures: mitochondria continually divide and fuse, changing their shape and connections. Damaged mitochondria can also be selectively removed through a process called mitophagy.

title: A Closer Look at Yeast
name: Yeast Cells
scientific: Differential interference contrast (DIC) microscopy image of yeast cells.
description: Yeast is a single-celled organism that has helped scientists understand many fundamental processes in biology. Because yeast cells are relatively simple to grow and study, they are widely used as model organisms in research. DIC microscopy enhances contrast, making the cells’ outlines and internal features easier to see.

title: A Wider View of the Cellular Landscape
name: Cell Scan
scientific: Wide-field fluorescence imaging of mitochondria (magenta), F-actin (green), and nuclei (cyan) in many BPAE cells from left to right scanning.
description: This moving view explores a larger area of the same types of BPAE cells in a broader cellular landscape and see how the labelled structures are distributed across the field.

title: A Panorama of the Cells
name: Cell Panorama
scientific: Wide-field fluorescence imaging of mitochondria (magenta), F-actin (green), and nuclei (cyan) in many BPAE cells from far to close look.
description: This movie presents a large region of the BPAE cells, offering a sense of scale and spatial organization.

title: Batman
description: Induction of definitive endoderm cells with specified soluble factors is the first step for stem cell differentiation toward beta cells. Partial activation of the canonical Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway triggers accumulation of β-catenin (magenta) in the cytoplasm of a subset cell population.

title: Super-resolution image of endocytic structures responsible for degrading intercellular junctions during sperm release in the testis
description: Cryo-section of rat testis with actin filaments (red) and actin networks stained around tubular endocytic structures along the concave surfaces of the cells. Also labelled are proteins (ORP9-blue; Myosin VI-green) associated with the ends of the structures.

title: Brainstorm
description: Organoid-Based COVID-19 Research: presented is the neuro-serine protease inhibitor (neuroserpin) Spn4A (cyan; discovered in the Jean lab) expressed in a human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived dorsal forebrain organoid. SARS-CoV-2 cell entry factors furin (red) and TMPRSS2 (green) are shown.

title: Neural Abstract Expressionism
description: Organoid-Based COVID-19 Research: Identifying Therapeutic Agents Using Lab-Grown Mini Brains. Presented here is the neuro-serine protease inhibitor (neuroserpin) Spn4A (cyan) discovered in the Jean lab. Human coronavirus cell entry factors, human aminopeptidase N (violet), and TMPRSS2 (green) are also shown.

title: New nasal spray treats Delta variant infection
lab: Labs: Drs. François Jean and Ivan R. Nabi, and the Life Sciences Institute Imaging Facility
department: Departments of Microbiology & Immunology, Cellular & Physiological Sciences, and Life Sciences Institute
description: SARS-CoV-2 B.1.617.2 (Delta Variant of Concern) infection induces a striking spheroid-like phenotype in Calu-3 cells (a non-small-cell lung cancer cell line). Host cell markers are nuclei (blue) and actin (cyan), while viral markers are dsRNA (red) and nucleocapsid (yellow).

title: The peripheral nerve of Drosophila larva
description: This single optical section shows the extracellular matrix (green) in close association with the peripheral perineurial glia (grey). The perineurial glia in turn enwrap the entire peripheral nerve with axonal tracts in the center (magenta).

title: Dream of Hydrangea
artists: Drs. Jia Zhao and Shenghui Liang
description: Stem cell-derived insulin-producing islets offer an unlimited cell source for therapeutic applications and unique opportunities for modeling diabetes in a dish. These manufactured stem cell-islets contain multiple islet cell types closely resembling native human islets and express important beta cell maturation markers.

title: Mish Mash
description: Disorganised embryonic muscles shown by the chaotic arrangement of actin filaments (white) in a Drosophila mutant affecting cell-extracellular matrix adhesion (Integrin in magenta).

title: Synapses in bloom at the neuromuscular junction
artists: Leila Abtahi and Dr. Robin Vuilleumier
description: Larval neuromuscular junction in Drosophila melanogaster. The boutons constitute synapses between neurons and muscles. Anti-Futsch staining in green. Futsch is a microtubule binding protein involved in the formation of synapses in flies. Neuronal membranes are labeled by anti-HRP (magenta).

title: Primary mouse embryonic fibroblast
description: Primary mouse embryonic fibroblast with Talin1 ABS3 mutations. The cell is stained for the actin cytoskeleton (fire LUT). The image was taken with a spinning disk confocal microscope and reveals a round cell shape with a chiral swirling actin organization pattern.
